https://www.politico.eu/article/friedric.text: BERLIN — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz doesn’t seem to think his job will be in danger when he gets back from his summer holiday. “I’m assuming that things will have calmed down a bit by September,” he said last week, after internal dissent over his handling of a cabinet reshuffle boiled over. He may be underestimating the pressure building within his own party. Advertisement Advertisement Ahead of crucial regional elections in September — in which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has a realistic chance of taking power in a German state for the first time — there is increasingly open discussion of a Kanzlertausch , or chancellor swap, in the fall. Public criticism has mainly come from those ousted from government in the reshuffle. But behind the scenes, a growing number of politicians from Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are discussing what would, by German standards, be a remarkable scenario: replacing the leader after little more than a year in the job. Europe’s biggest economy has long been one of its most stable democracies, with no history of rattling through leaders like postwar Italy or post-Brexit Britain. But the expected success of the AfD, in elections in which the CDU is expected to lose ground, is upending the country’s conventional political dynamics. The theory behind a Kanzlertausch is that the conservatives will need to stem the fallout from the eastern elections and give themselves a boost by replacing a leader unable to shake his rock-bottom ratings. But the stakes are high. The AfD — now the most popular party in national polls — would seek to capitalize on further coalition unrest. Replacing a chancellor years before the end of his term would mean venturing into largely uncharted political territory. Advertisement Advertisement Only three sitting chancellors have been succeeded by a politician from the same political camp in postwar Germany: in 1963, when the 87-year-old Konrad Adenauer resigned to make way for Ludwig Erhard; in 1966, after Erhard’s coalition collapsed ; and in 1974, when Social Democrat Willy Brandt stood down over an espionage scandal. The current Kanzlertausch scenario — in which Hendrik Wüst, the premier of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, has emerged as Merz’s most likely successor — has been widely discussed in German media, including in the latest Der Spiegel cover story headlined “ Palace Revolt .” Conservative politicians confirmed the internal debate to POLITICO, speaking on condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the discussions. The AfD — now the most popular party in national polls — would seek to capitalize on further coalition unrest. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images The growing discontent, they said, reflected declining trust in the chancellor’s statesmanship and his expected inability to keep the party together if the AfD takes power in September. Polls show that the AfD could win an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6, while it is poised to win in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and do well in Berlin on Sept. 20. A further fear is that individual CDU politicians in eastern Germany might lend their support to an AfD-led state government after the elections — breaking Merz’s long-standing pledge never to allow the far right into government. Advertisement Advertisement One called the debate “speculative” for now and said that the aftermath of the elections in eastern Germany would be “decisive” for the chancellor’s future. They also stressed that, for now, no senior figure has publicly spoken out against Merz. Yet the mounting unease is conspicuous in a party usually known for its discipline. Keeping a cool head If Merz were forced to go, that would seriously disrupt Germany’s consensus-based political system. The move would come less than two years after the previous center-left coalition fell apart and could trigger a snap election. Kai Arzheimer, a political science professor at the University of Mainz, said the fragmentation of Germany’s party system — where centrist parties must forge sometimes awkward coalitions to keep increasingly popular fringe parties from power — has triggered a shift. “Compared with the 1970s and 1980s, Germany has experienced relatively little political stability for quite some time now,” he said. “However, by the standards of what has become the norm in many other European countries, one could also say that Germany has simply arrived where others have been for a long time.” Advertisement Advertisement Appeals for restraint have meanwhile begun to emerge from across the political spectrum. “A Union that is tearing itself apart is of no use to anyone in the democratic center,” said Christiane Hoffmann, a former spokesperson for center-left Chancellor Olaf Scholz, in a lengthy post on X about the current debate. “I am firmly convinced that Friedrich Merz will remain chancellor,” Markus Söder said. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images “A little stability, please,” she demanded. “There’s just headless grumbling and bleating, with no one knowing where it’s all headed. Europe is on fire. Could a few people please keep a cool head?” How a swap could unfold The least disruptive route would be for Merz to step aside voluntarily, allowing his successor to be elected by majority vote. If Merz refuses to go, his opponents would have to oust him through a constructive vote of no confidence, simultaneously electing his successor. Such an extraordinary parliamentary maneuver would risk ripping apart the governing coalition of Merz’s CDU, its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and the Social Democrats. For now, Merz continues to enjoy the backing of leading conservative figures. Advertisement Advertisement “I am firmly convinced that Friedrich Merz will remain chancellor,” Markus Söder, the powerful state premier of Bavaria and CSU leader, said in an interview with public broadcaster ARD over the weekend. “It would throw the conservatives into complete disarray,” Söder said of a potential swap. “Moreover, it could even lead to new elections. And anyone who wants new elections now — in a situation like this, after such a lead-up — is only promoting one thing: bringing radicals to power. That is why my urgent advice is to focus on the work at hand and spend less time speculating behind the scenes.” At national level, POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts the AfD as the single most popular party with 28 percent support, with Merz’s conservatives on 21 percent. At the same time, only 13 percent of Germans are satisfied with Merz’s performance, according to the latest benchmark ARD-DeutschlandTrend poll released last month . That is the lowest rating for a sitting chancellor in the survey’s nearly 30-year history. Merz’s rock-bottom ratings reflect disappointment over his efforts to revive Germany’s ailing economy and public skepticism over far-reaching pension and health care reforms that will be difficult to implement and are expected to cost the average voter money. For now, Merz’s most viable political strategy appears to be appealing to politicians’ risk aversion in an effort to preserve what remains of Germany’s reputation for political stability. “I can’t imagine many people within the conservative camp saying: ‘This is the solution, and we’re willing to take any risk in the hope that we might then do better in the polls,’” said Arzheimer, the political science professor. “That would be a completely crazy idea.” Advertisement

Beállítom “Acting on my instructions, on Tuesday the relevant official from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed the Russian ambassador to Hungary that, according to the assessment of the Hungarian authorities, 10 members of the Russian mission had engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention. The Hungarian side has therefore called on the individuals in question to leave Hungary. This decision protects Hungary’s security and sovereignty”-- Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced on her Facebook page. An expulsion of this magnitude is unprecedented; never before have so many Russian diplomats been sent home from the country. The Minister added that the move “does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules.” The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded to the news by saying: Russia will respond to the expulsion of 10 of its diplomats from Hungary. According to Maria Zakharova, the spokeswoman for the Russian Foreign Ministry,, “the response will be harsh and painful”. Prime Minister Péter Magyar read out Anita Orbán’s statement in Parliament, and said that the Tisza government would defend the country’s sovereignty. We have sent questions to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to find out when it was that the Hungarian authorities realized that the 10 embassy staff members were engaging in activities "unacceptable for diplomats". In its response, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated that for the time being, they do not wish to share any further information about the expulsions. We also contacted the Russian Embassy in Budapest to ask for their comment on the decision of the Hungarian Minister of Foreign Affairs, and inquired whether a diplomatic response is expected. Compared to her predecessor Péter Szijjártó, Anita Orbán has maintained a much more reserved diplomatic relationship with Russia. In the early days of her tenure as minister, on May 13, after Moscow launched a drone attack against Transcarpathia (Ukraine’s region home to a significant Hungarian ethnic minority) she summoned the Russian ambassador to Budapest. In comparison, the last time Szijjártó had summoned a Russian diplomat was in February 2022. Also in May, VSquare reported that after the Hungarian election, a Russian intelligence officer working under diplomatic cover was quietly expelled from Hungary. Artur Sushkov left Hungary on May 4; according to the VSquare article, Hungary expelled him after the Constitution Protection Office (AH) discovered that, as an intelligence officer working under diplomatic cover at the Russian Embassy in Budapest, he had for years been gathering information on institutions close to the government. According to VSquare's sources close to the government, Hungarian intelligence had recommended Suskov's expulsion as early as February, but the Orbán government blocked the move. In a post reacting to the fresh expulsion, investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi wrote that, to his knowledge, there had only been a few “quiet expulsions” under the previous Hungarian government. In addition to Artur Sushkov, the other quiet expulsion—which is only now coming to light—took place on June 20, 2024, when Andrei Tarakanov, a third secretary and GRU officer operating under diplomatic cover, was sent back to Moscow. According to Panyi, Tarakanov barely spent a year in Hungary—he arrived in August 2023—and, according to a source familiar with his activities, he was not involved in Russian influence operations targeting Hungary, but rather ones aimed at other EU member states. The Orbán government expelled a Russian diplomat in 2018, but neither side’s interests were harmed In 2018, the Orbán government was among the countries which expelled a Russian diplomat; however, as Direkt36 discovered, there was no real tension behind the scenes. Like many Western countries at the time, Hungary also decided to show solidarity with the United Kingdom following the poisoning of Sergei Skripal, a former Russian spy living in Britain, and to expel a Russian diplomat. This was not only remarkable because of the two countries’ good relations, but also because several other European Union member states did not expel anyone. Moreover, there had been no precedent in Hungary for the official expulsion of a Russian diplomat under the Orbán governments which had been in power since 2010. However, an investigation by Direkt36 revealed that Hungary’s response to the Skripal case was in fact deliberately orchestrated so as not to jeopardize the special relationship between the two countries. At that time, Direkt36 learned from several diplomatic sources that the GRU (military intelligence) officer Hungary had expelled was working under diplomatic cover at the Russian Embassy in Budapest, and their posting would have expired within a few months anyway. In return, Moscow decided to send home a Hungarian foreign economic attaché who held a position of no particular importance. European countires started expelling Russian diplomats in large numbers and very publicly beginning in 2018, following the poisoning of Sergei Skripal. At that time, 25 EU and NATO member states expelled more than 125 Russian diplomats within a month. Three years later, following the 2014 ammunition depot explosion, the Czech Republic sent 18 staff members of the Russian embassy home and six other countries subsequently expelled more than 25. Following the launch of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, European countries moved to expel Russian diplomats in unprecedented numbers. In April 2022, more than 200 Russian diplomats were expelled from Europe within just two days as part of a coordinated response to the Bucha massacre. Over the course of two months, 25 EU and NATO countries ordered more than 400 diplomats to leave, with Poland, Germany, and France expelling the most—40 each. Only a handful of NATO member states did not participate in the effort at the time, some—such as the United Kingdom—because they had already expelled large numbers of Russian diplomats beforehand. By mid-May, more than 450 Russian embassy staff members had been expelled. According to an August article in the German newspaper Bild, Berlin has expelled 80 Russian diplomats since February 2022, the last one in January of this year; according to the article, most of them were agents disguised as diplomats. This year, Austria expelled three Russian diplomats suspected of espionage, bringing the total number of Russian diplomats expelled by Austria since 2020 to 14. In July, the Italian Foreign Minister announced that two Russian military attachés had been expelled on charges of espionage. Polish Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski stated last week that the EU should expel even more Russian diplomats following the attempted drone-bomb attack at the Leipzig Airport. After a meeting with the French and German foreign ministers last Thursday, Sikorski said that there are too many Russian diplomats in the European Union, noting that, according to their estimates, roughly 40 percent of the more than 2,000 Russian diplomats are “performing tasks that are incompatible with their diplomatic status,” adding that “they work for agencies that also carry out terrorist acts in our countries.” For more quick, accurate and impartial news from and about Hungary, subscribe to the Telex English newsletter! https://www.countytimes.co.uk/news/26505.text: Caernarfon Crown Court Murder Court Crime Welshpool Welshpool murder accused denies charge before trial By Anwen Parry Chief Reporter Share 4 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A man accused of murdering a 49-year-old who was found seriously injured in a Welshpool street has denied the charge and is set to stand trial later this year. Young John Mongan , from Walsall, died after emergency services were called to Church Street, Welshpool, at around 1.15am on June 28. Despite the efforts of paramedics, he died at the scene. Martin Slezak , 23, of Stanley Street, Welshpool , is charged in connection with Mr Mongan's death. A murder investigation was launched after a man died in Welshpool in the early hours of Sunday morning, June 28. (Image: Matt Jones) Appearing before Caernarfon Crown Court by video link from HMP Berwyn on Friday, August 28, Slezak entered a not guilty plea to murder before Mr Justice Nicklin KC. Prosecutor Mr Bull told the court that both sides would be ready for a trial beginning on November 9. The trial is expected to last two weeks. During the hearing, defence barrister Philip Clemo said the precise nature of the defence would be set out in a defence statement. Asked whether the defence would be offering a plea to an alternative charge, Mr Clemo replied: "Not at this stage." Forensic investigators in Welshpool, after police opened a murder investigation into the death of a man in the town centre. (Image: Matt Jones) Flowers have been left in memory of Young John Mongan in Church Street. (Image: Ruairi Walsh) The judge also approved an application for special measures for Mr Mongan's widow, Margaret Mongan, when she gives evidence. The defence raised no objection. The court heard that Polish and Turkish interpreters may be required during the trial. Slezak was assisted by a Polish interpreter during Friday's hearing. As part of trial preparations, the court discussed several witnesses expected to give evidence, although the defence said it hoped to reduce that number before the case reaches trial. Remanding Slezak in custody until November, Mr Justice Nicklin set a timetable of further case management hearings through September and October. The trial is due to begin at Caernarfon Crown Court on November 9. Caernarfon Crown Court Murder Court Crime Welshpool Share Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading... https://www.dw.com/en/bulgaria-holds-pre.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OdWi Bulgarians are deciding on who should officially reside here in Sofia Image: Dzhanan Mehmed Ismail/Anadolu/IMAGO Advertisement Bulgarians are going to the polls in a presidential election on Sunday , where they are choosing between candidates who differ on their approach to the war in Ukraine and how close the country should draw to Moscow. The vote comes as drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea off the Bulgarian coast have brought home the significance of the conflict in Ukraine for the former Soviet satellite state. Polling stations are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. (0500-1800 GMT), with exit polls to be released when they close. Official results are expected up to 48 hours after voting ends. Although the presidency is largely ceremonial, the head of state in Bulgaria can appoint interim governments during political crises, is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and is able to veto legislation. How Russian aggression is shaping Bulgaria's presidential election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Who are the main candidates in Bulgaria's presidential election? Frontrunner in the elections is incumbent President Iliana Iotova, who took over the position this year after current Prime Minister Rumen Radev stepped down to take part in the parliamentary elections that led him to power. Iotova, 62, who surveys show as having 41-47% of the vote, favors dialogue with Moscow as the way to bring peace to Ukraine and opposes military aid to Kyiv. A win for Iotova would give a boost for Radev, who also advocates dialogue with Moscow. Her main challenger is Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister, who is polling at 28-31%. Gyurov, 50, who is backed by the pro-Western opposition, is an outspoken critic of Radev's foreign policy and strongly supports the Euro-Atlantic ties of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state. The leader of the pro-Russian far-right Vazrazhdane party, Kostadin Kostadinov, is in third place on 10-13%. Altogether 27 pairs of candidates for president and vice president are competing in the first round, with nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin. If no candidate wins an absolute majority in the first round, a run-off is scheduled for November 1, with Iotova and Gyurov widely considered as the certain contenders in any second round. Iotova (R) appointed Gyurov (L) as caretaker premier, a post he held from February to March 2026 Image: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance What are the main issues in Bulgaria's presidential election? The war in Ukraine triggered by Russia's unprovoked invasion is one of the central themes in the election, particularly after four merchant ships were allegedly hit by drones off Bulgaria's coast this month in suspected spillover from the conflict. Satellite internet antennas from the Starlink network — an important part of Ukraine's defense capabilities — were also set on fire near the capital, Sofia. While Radev has said that the attacks seemed to be to the advantage of Russia and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government has declined to blame the incidents directly on Moscow. The strikes have nonetheless raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict. Rising energy prices and inflation that have caused economic hardship to many in Bulgaria, the EU's poorest member state, are also a main issue addressed by candidates. Many voters are also looking to stop government corruption, a persistent concern in the country, and hope for a stable government after multiple elections and coalition breakdowns in recent years.
